text.p: Fund investors have had such success lately that they've begun to forget what it's like to lose money. In fact, the last year that stock funds as a group lost money was 1994, when they declined a piddling 1.37 percent.
But before you get the idea that it's easy to avoid losses in stocks, consider this fact: Only one equity fund has gone 21 calendar years without a losing year.
The fund is FPA Paramount (800-982-4372; $1,500 minimum investment; 6.5 percent load), which recently reopened to new investors.

Chances are, it won't be open for long. The fund first closed its doors in 1983, and investors since then have had only two brief opportunities, totalling seven months, to buy its shares. Should you take this chance to invest in the fund before its doors slam shut again?

Maybe so. The fund's manager, Bill Sams, is one of the most respected contrarians in the investment business. His strategy is to look for truly out-of-favour stocks and industries, and invest in them for the long term. His success depends in part upon his ability to spot talented managers who can turn around troubled companies.

Case in point: Sams' decision to invest in International Business Machines Corp. when its shares declined during 1995 was based in part on his belief that Chief Executive Lou Gerstner could turn the company around.

It's a risky approach in the wrong hands, and Sams compounds the fund's potential risk by holding just 20 or 30 stocks at a time; that compares with hundreds of stocks for the typical fund. If a few of his picks blow up, the portfolio could suffer badly -- but they generally don't.
In fact, the fund has been only about three-quarters as volatile as the typical growth and income fund during the past five years, according to Morningstar Inc.

Performance? The fund ranks second among 123 growth and income funds tracked by Lipper Analytical Services during the past decade; and it's first among 81 funds for the past 15 years. Last year, the fund gained 29 percent, putting it in the top 5 percent of all growth-and-income entries, despite its considerable cash holdings, which recently accounted for 30 percent of the portfolio.
These days, many of the hottest funds have been run by managers who are willing to chase top-performing stocks.

Such "momentum" investing has worked extremely well during the past several years. As a result, many funds managed by inexperienced managers have performed very well. But when the market declines, the biggest losses will occur among the most popular market sectors -- the ones that Sams consistently avoids.
Sams says that despite the market's recent gains, there are still some cheap stocks around. Typically, they are shares of companies that investors perceive as troubled.
"Those stocks have lost their weakest holders already," he said. "So fresh bad news doesn't have as much impact on them, and unexpected good news can send them soaring."

One recent pick was Amdahl Corp., the computer hardware and software supplier. Investors aren't interested now, because the company's earnings growth isn't especially strong. But Sams sees them getting stronger as the company moves from relying on hardware to relying more on service, a faster-growing area.

He also likes gold mines, one of the few domestic stock groups to post a loss in 1996. In January he purchased his first-ever gold mining stock: Homestake Mining. He figures international economic growth will boost demand for the metal going forward. What's more, the stocks are extremely cheap in this market, which makes them even more precious in Sams' eyes.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
